title: Adaptive learning systems for English literature classrooms: A review of AI-integrated education platforms
venue: International Journal of Scientific Interdisciplinary Research
extended_summary:
This paper examines the role of adaptive learning systems integrated with artificial intelligence in English Literature education. It asks how AI-enabled adaptive platforms can personalize instruction, improve comprehension and interpretive analysis, support writing development, and reshape teacher practice in literature classrooms. The article is positioned as a systematic review, following PRISMA guidelines, and synthesizes findings from 94 peer-reviewed studies across multiple educational settings.

The review focuses on adaptive platforms that adjust pacing, text difficulty, feedback, and scaffolding based on learner performance. It highlights technological components such as natural language processing, learner modeling, writing analytics, recommendation engines, and adaptive sequencing. The paper emphasizes use cases in native-English, EFL/ESL, bilingual, and resource-constrained contexts, including K-12 and higher education, with attention to text-first, writing-first, and hybrid platform typologies.

Across the reviewed studies, the authors conclude that AI-integrated adaptive systems generally improve reading comprehension, interpretive accuracy, intertextual awareness, writing quality, metacognitive awareness, engagement, and equity of access. The review also argues that these systems complement rather than replace teachers, who shift toward facilitation, interpretation, and discussion leadership. Overall, the paper presents adaptive learning as a pedagogically grounded and scalable innovation for literature education, especially when aligned with curricular goals and accessibility needs.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/systematic review of prior literature, not a primary causal study, RCT, or meta-analysis with extracted pooled estimates. Although it follows PRISMA, the provided text does not report a transparent quantitative synthesis or study-level credibility assessment sufficient for a higher evidence tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The review describes consistently positive impacts of adaptive literature systems, but the paper does not report a pooled effect size or direct causal estimate. The magnitude of impact is therefore unclear at the paper level, even though the overall direction across the literature is positive.

interventions.use_case: AI-integrated adaptive learning systems for English Literature instruction, including personalized reading pathways, scaffolded interpretive prompts, adaptive sequencing, dashboards, and progress monitoring
Automated feedback on literary essays and short responses, including thesis clarity, evidence integration, coherence, and iterative revision support
NLP-supported writing and language scaffolds for literature learners, including vocabulary support, discourse markers, translation/cultural notes, and writing analytics
Software-delivered adaptive close-reading, question ladders, and scaffolded annotation activities for literature comprehension and analysis

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that adaptive learning systems consistently improved literacy-related outcomes in English Literature classrooms, including reading comprehension, device recognition, interpretive accuracy, intertextual connections, and writing quality. Across the synthesized studies (n=94 papers reviewed), adaptive scaffolds and automated feedback were reported to support iterative revision, thesis clarity, and evidence integration, although the paper does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, literary device recognition, interpretive accuracy, intertextual reasoning, and writing quality/essay revision

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that adaptive systems increased engagement, time on task, enjoyment of literature, and perceived relevance by personalizing challenge and reducing frustration. These effects are described qualitatively across the reviewed literature rather than as a pooled estimate, but the direction is consistently positive.
finding.measure: Engagement, time on task, enjoyment, perceived relevance

finding.finding_summary: Adaptive dashboards, reflective prompts, and progress monitoring were described as supporting metacognition and self-regulated learning in literature study. The review also notes gains in critical thinking and interpretive dialogue through scaffolded questioning and collaborative discussion, but does not provide quantitative pooled effects.
finding.measure: Metacognitive awareness, self-regulated learning, critical thinking, collaborative interpretation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that adaptive systems can reduce performance gaps for lower-proficiency learners, bilingual learners, learners with disabilities, and students in low-resource contexts through linguistic scaffolds, inclusive features, and offline/mobile functionality. It also reports that teacher roles shift toward facilitation and interpretive dialogue, suggesting institutional benefits in classroom orchestration, but these claims are synthesized from prior studies rather than estimated in a single causal analysis.
finding.measure: Equity/accessibility outcomes, teacher role reconfiguration, access in low-resource settings
